beginner.summary: For web, API and integration developers who have used a "Sign in with" button but have never read the specifications behind it. Covers OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect from the protocol side: the four OAuth roles, the authorization code flow with PKCE, state and nonce, ID token validation, UserInfo, scopes and standard claims, discovery and JWKS, client authentication, the client credentials, refresh token and device authorization grants, bearer tokens at an API, consent and the prompt parameter, introspection and revocation, standard error responses, and a capstone that adds OIDC login and API access to a small web app. Every lab runs against a local Keycloak realm used only as a test OpenID Provider, with curl, jq and a browser.
prerequisites: Builds and runs a small web application or HTTP API in a language such as JavaScript, Python, Java or C#
Reads HTTP requests and responses: methods, status codes, headers, query strings, form bodies and redirects
Has Docker, curl, jq and a modern browser with developer tools on a laptop with rights to run containers on port 8080
outcomes: Explain the OAuth 2.0 roles, endpoints and grants and say which grant suits a web app, a service, a device or a script
Run the authorization code flow with PKCE, state and nonce by hand and validate the resulting ID token claim by claim
Use discovery, JWKS, UserInfo, introspection and revocation endpoints and read standard OAuth and OIDC error responses
Add OpenID Connect login and bearer-token API calls to a web application using a certified client library

intermediate.summary: For developers and identity engineers who can already run the authorization code flow with PKCE and validate an ID token, and now need to design and operate OAuth and OIDC across several client types and APIs. Covers OAuth 2.1 and the Security BCP (RFC 9700), the claims parameter, acr_values and max_age, pairwise subjects, dynamic client registration, authorization server metadata and resource indicators, the JWT access token profile, scope and audience design, RP-initiated, back-channel and front-channel logout, the backend-for-frontend pattern for single-page apps, native, mobile and CLI clients, refresh token rotation policy, step-up authentication, and how Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, Google and Keycloak differ as OpenID Providers.

Has built at least one web application and one API that use OAuth 2.0 access tokens
Can run Docker containers and Node.js or Python code locally, and has a free developer tenant for at least one of Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0 or Google Cloud
